paras: The attempted lynching of Louis Everson took place in Dearborn County, Indiana, on 23-25 May 1903, when crowds of farmers threatened to lynch Everson, a Black man known as "Black Ponto," held in the Lawrenceburg jail on suspicion of murdering Rosa Kaiser. No witness identified him; after his release a mob stoned, beat and fired at him; one report said a mob tried to lynch him near Aurora. Black papers reported the murder and the drive against Black residents that followed it, but did not name him.

Rosa Kaiser and her elderly father, Martin Kaiser, were attacked near Manchester Station while walking home from church; he was clubbed, and posses with bloodhounds hunted a Black man said to have been seen nearby. Her body was found in a branch of Tanner's creek on 23 May, and the coroner's verdict blamed persons unknown, "believed to have been two negroes seen acting suspiciously" near the scene. Everson, described by the Indianapolis Journal as an ex-convict wanted at Rising Sun for "cutting with intent to kill," had been arrested at Cleves, Ohio, and denied any part in the attack.

Fearing trouble near the scene, Sheriff Axby brought Everson to the Lawrenceburg jail on 23 May "for protection," and that night he doubled the guard and barricaded the building as farmers filled the town. According to the Courier-Journal, crowds roamed the streets all night making threats against the prisoner's life, held back only by uncertainty about his guilt. On 24 May farmers gathered at Lawrenceburg, Guilford, Manchester and other towns and "openly threatened lynching if the guilty person could be identified." The Associated Press reported "no doubt" that he would have been lynched that day had Albert Darling and other neighbors from Manchester not failed to identify him.

On the evening of 25 May, after Rising Sun withdrew its old warrant, Sheriff Axby and two officers walked Everson down the Big Four tracks beyond the city limits and told him to "make himself scarce." A "hooting mob of men and boys" followed him for about a mile, cursing, stoning and beating him, and the Courier-Journal added that shots were fired after him. A late telephone message said a mob had tried to lynch him near Aurora and that he escaped by swimming Hogan's creek.

Rearrested at Dillsboro on 26 May, Everson was released again at once. By then Martin Kaiser and an uncle were said to believe the killer was a white man, and in September the sheriff was seeking another suspect, Otto Pool. No report of an arrest of anyone who threatened or attacked Everson appears in the coverage.

Rosa Kaiser's brother Louis circulated a petition asking the Big Four contractors to dismiss their Black laborers, and later reports described Black families ordered out of the county and seven families near Manchester Station driven from their homes.

Indianapolis and Louisville specials and an Associated Press dispatch, reprinted from Indiana to Nebraska and Utah and in German translation, carried the story. Headlines included "Mob After a Negro" in the Deseret Evening News, "Farmers Are Agitated" in the Madison Daily Leader and "Negro Chased Out of Town by Mob" in the Courier-Journal. Early reports leaned toward his guilt; the Wheeling Sunday Register wrote that "He is believed to be guilty and a lynching may follow," and the wire accounts explained the crowds' restraint by doubt about his identity rather than by the law. After the release the Indianapolis Journal conceded that no incriminating evidence had been found, yet predicted he would be "tarred and feathered" if he stayed, and a day later headlined "May Have Been White Man."

The Black papers in the collection did not mention Everson. The Baltimore Afro-American noted only that Rosa Kaiser had been "brutally assaulted and killed by some brute," while the Savannah Tribune headlined the aftermath "Making War on Negroes."

Accounts of the release differ: the Indianapolis Journal's correspondent cited the withdrawn Rising Sun warrant, while wire briefs said Martin Kaiser had failed to identify Everson, though one noted that Kaiser never saw his assailant. The Aurora lynching attempt rests on one telephone report; the Courier-Journal describes the stoning and shots but no lynching attempt.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Louis Everson
bases: Crowds of farmers threatened to lynch Everson while he was jailed on suspicion of murder (A3, A5, A6), and after his release a mob stoned, beat and shot at him and reportedly tried to lynch him (A10, A11, A12).

Everson was threatened, stoned, beaten and shot at by crowds and a 'mob of men and boys' acting on suspicion of the Kaiser murder (A5, A10, A12), but he escaped and was rearrested alive on 26 May (A16); it was an attempted lynching, not a killing.

The jail threats are reported independently by Indianapolis Journal and Courier-Journal specials and the Associated Press (A2, A3, A5, A6), and the stoning and beating by both the Journal and the Courier-Journal (A10, A12); only the Aurora lynching attempt rests on a single telephone report (A11).

accounts.gist: Reported the murder and the campaign to drive Black families and workers out of Dearborn County, without naming Everson.

framing.detail: Early reports presumed guilt ('He is believed to be guilty and a lynching may follow'; lynching or burning 'can scarcely be avoided'); after the release the Journal ran 'Negro Suspect Is Freed' and 'May Have Been White Man.'
The AP dispatch ran as 'Mob After a Negro', 'Farmers Are Agitated' and in German translation, treating the threats as conditional on identification.
The Courier-Journal headlined 'Negro Chased Out of Town by Mob' and described the stoning and shooting without comment.
The Savannah Tribune headlined the expulsions 'Making War on Negroes'; neither Black paper mentioned Everson.
